                    Bodies


       HIS CHAPTER DESCRIBES THE equipment needed to silver solder
      small ceramic burners successfully, and how to undertake the
      process. It includes some basic information about liquefiedT
petroleum gases, including safety instructions, and describes
suitable torches for heating the metal parts, techniques for silver
soldering, suitable hearths, and methods of chemically cleaning the
parts of the burner once silver soldering is complete.

GAS FOR SILVER SOLDERING

You will need to use liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to provide the
heat for silver soldering. LPG is a fossil fuel closely linked to oil, and
is used in many applications including heating. The gas has a
powerful odorant added so that leaks are easily detected from the
smell. It is flammable, and heavier (denser) than air, so it settles and
accumulates in low spots. Serious leaks can present a fire hazard, or
even the risk of an explosion.

FIG. 34
 A 13kg bottle of propane carries enough gas to solder the bodies of hundreds of ceramic
                                        burners.

  LPG under pressure is available in portable cylinders. When
compressed, it readily changes to a liquid, so a large amount of gas
can be stored in a relatively small space. However, in order to be

burned the LPG must be able to boil, expanding significantly to form
a gas. Propane is supplied in a range of cylinder sizes of which
those suitable for use in home workshops contain either 6kg or 13kg
of the liquid gas and will power a torch with a small nozzle for a very
long time. Figure 34 shows a typical cylinder. Propane cylinders
connect to torches through fittings with left-hand threads.





                                      FIG. 35
   A MAP (methylacetylene-propadiene) gas torch screwed on to a MAP gas cylinder.

For silver soldering, propane is the gas normally employed by
model engineers, though MAPP gas – methylacetylene-propadiene
propane – is a useful alternative where relatively small amounts of
heat are required, such as when making ceramic burners. It is also
called MAP gas. It burns at just over 2,000ºC, whereas propane
burns at a little below that figure. The increased temperature and the
design of MAPPgas burners help to simplify silver soldering small
items such as the bodies of ceramic burners. Figure 35 is a photo of
a MAP-gas torch. The cylinders for MAP gas contain a nominal 400g
(14oz) of gas, and although it is at least 50 per cent more expensive
than propane, not much gas is used when making a burner.



  BASIC SAFETY NOTICE

   Most of you will hate ‘health and safety’ warnings, but the best
   advice for all model engineers is to read any warning and
   remember to be careful – as careful as you would be when
   dealing with gas or electricity in your home or petrol in your
    car. You need to observe some safety precautions when using
   propane or MAP gas, which are both forms of LPG, for silver
   soldering.

  ■ LPG is denser than air. Any leaking gases will pool on your
     workshop floor so it is essential to check that your
     connecters and pipework are correctly installed and do not
      leak. You should frequently inspect all of them. In warmer
     weather, you should consider silver soldering in a shady
     outdoor place – though be aware this will make it harder to
     judge when the item you are soldering is coming up to red
     heat

■ Always carefully turn off the gas at the cylinder at the end of
     each soldering session. If you are using a propane torch,
     disconnect the pipes from the gas cylinder once you have
      finished soldering
  ■ Inevitably your gas torch will heat up metal quickly – and
     your skin if you are not careful. So do wear a pair of
      protective gloves when silver soldering. Even with the torch
       off for a couple of minutes, its metal can still burn you
      painfully if you touch it
  ■ Be careful if you use dilute sulphuric acid as a pickle. Never
    add water to acid, only ever add acid to water. Wear
      protective clothes, gloves and a face mask. If you do get
     acid on your skin or clothes, quickly wash it off with water.
    And only dispose of the acid after neutralizing it with baking
     powder


TORCHES FOR SILVER SOLDERING

You will need some facilities for silver soldering to make any of the
burners. You may already have some silver solder and flux, as well
as a gas torch. The two practical alternatives are a propane gas
torch and cylinder with a choice of nozzle sizes, or a MAPP gas
torch where the burner head screws on to the top of the small gas
cylinder. The head also contains a piezo-electric ignition system.

FIG. 36
  A Sievert gas torch; any of the smallest three burners will provide adequate heat when
                            making ceramic burners.

   The low mass of the metal used in ceramic burners means that
they do not require a huge amount of heat to raise their temperature
sufficiently to silver solder them. Thus a propane gas torch (like the
one in Figure 36) is, perhaps, overkill for making ceramic burners –
but such a torch will have many other uses including building steam
boilers to power locomotives, traction engines, lorries or static steam

engines. You need to be aware that small DIY butane-powered gas
torches used for soft soldering will not provide sufficient heat for
silver soldering.

SILVER SOLDERING

It is essential to realize that soft solder is unsuitable for making the
burners in this book because it has little or no strength at the
temperatures experienced in a burner body. Even worse, a joint
failure could cause a gas leak, which is also potentially dangerous.
Finally, it is worth remembering that any metal that has been soft
soldered cannot then be silver soldered. For those who have already
built a boiler, silver soldering a burner should provide no problems.
For those who are inexperienced, it is not difficult to become
proficient at silver soldering, and making burners is an ideal place to
start acquiring the techniques. The following are a few important
issues that must be learned:

ISSUE 1: All the parts of the burner that are to be silver soldered
must be completely clean. This means removing any oxides, grease
(including finger marks), oil and dirt. As a minimum, this involves
cleaning well with wire wool until the metal shines. Seriously stained
metal can be pickled and then washed in water to clean it.

FIG. 37
Lengths of 1.5 × 500mm Silver-Flo SF55 solder that is cadmium free. It is the ideal silver
                         solder for making any of the burners.

FIG. 38
 Easy-flo flux comes in powdered form in various sizes of plastic container, ready for mixing
                                        with water.

ISSUE 2: It is essential to use the right silver solder and flux. Silver-
Flo 55, lengths of which are shown in Figure 37, is today the
preferred, non-cadmium bearing, relatively low-temperature silver
solder and Easy-Flo is an ideal flux. Figure 38 shows pots of the flux
powder. The solder has a melting range of 630°C–660°C, flows well
and provides moderate fillets.
   Brush Easy-Flo 2 flux around the edges of every joint. The
powdered flux should be mixed with water and one drop of washing-
up liquid so the flux spreads easily on the bare metal, stirring until
the mixture has the consistency of thick cream. Only a small amount

of flux will be needed, and only part of a 600mm length of 1.5mm
Silver-Flo 55 to make any one of the eleven different burners.
   For soldering copper gas-pipe connections, it is easier not to
apply too much solder if a thinner rod or solder wire can be used.
Regardless, silver solder is expensive to buy so take care not to
waste it.

ISSUE 3: A suitable heat source that provides sufficient but not
excessive heat should be used. For building ceramic burners, a
relatively low-cost, self-contained MAPP gas torch, if you have
access to one, is ideal. However, if you already have a propane
torch, you can use a small nozzle on this type of torch and can run it
from a large propane gas cylinder. And do wear heat-resistant gloves
to avoid burning your fingers.





                                      FIG. 39
 If you have the space, you can create a simple hearth from Thermalite blocks on a bench in
               your workshop or on top of a Black and Decker Workmate.

FIG. 40
An old firebrick 200mm (8in) square is sufficiently large for silver soldering a burner.

FIG. 41
 A well-cleaned 35mm burner on a firebrick supported by pieces of Scanalex and ready for
                                          soldering.

ISSUE 4: You will need a small hearth made of Thermalite or similar
blocks (see Figure 39), or just a firebrick, shown in Figure 40, or
even a piece of vermiculite board on which to place the burner parts
that are to be soldered together. So paint the flux around the joints
that are to be soldered, and place the parts on the hearth, with the

burner tube supported on a thin piece of fireproof material. This is
demonstrated in Figure 41. Vermiculite board, Scamolex or
Skamolex, a vermiculite-based board, is ideal for this and can be
sawn and filed to size.





                                      FIG. 42
 The 35mm burner metal is red hot and the solder is flowing nicely around the join between
                     the jet-holder housing and the smaller end cap.

FIG. 43
 The 42mm burner showing how the silver solder has flashed around the joint between its
                                 two end caps.

  Now heat the metal parts until they are red hot. You will see the
flux sizzle and then go clear, and the metal parts will return to their
shiny colours as red heat is reached. (It is advisable to avoid silver
soldering in direct sunlight as it is difficult to see when the metal
reaches red heat.) A light touch of silver solder rod on each joint,
which has first been briefly heated in the flame and then dipped in
the powdered flux, should result in the solder melting and flashing

around your joint. This can be seen in Figures 42 and 43. Do not
overheat the parts to be joined. Overheating can prevent the flux
working effectively, and the solder from flowing around the joint.





                                      FIG. 44
       Repairing a corner joint on the large rectangular burner to ensure a good seal.

ISSUE 5: After cleaning the burner, carefully inspect it to ensure that
all joints are filled with solder and gas tight. Any doubtful joints
should be re-fluxed and then re-soldered and finally re-cleaned.
Figure 44 shows the corner of a rectangular burner that has been
cleaned and is being reheated to improve the seal on a corner joint.

Sifbronze Brazing

Because silver solder is expensive due to its high silver content,
experiments were made using Sifbronze, a brass (despite its name)
brazing alloy that is much cheaper. It does, however, have a much

higher melting temperature of 875°C–895°C than silver solder, and it
resulted in brass components in the burner melting. It is therefore not
recommended for making ceramic burners. Silver solder is by far the
best solution, and you will not use much.

CLEANING AND PICKLING

Some cleaning of the burner will be necessary once you have
completed the soldering but before fitting any gas-diffusing
components or the ceramic. This is readily done in a pickle of either
citric or dilute sulphuric acid. Figure 45 shows a burner body after
pickling. However, you must wait until the burner is completely cool
before putting in any pickle.





                                      FIG. 45
After cleaning in pickle and washing, carefully check all the joints. This is particularly vital on
                                              all rectangular burners.

FIG. 46
Citric acid is a safer but slower-acting pickle; it is widely available in crystal form that readily
                          dissolves in water to produce the acid.

FIG. 47
   Sulphuric acid is a highly corrosive liquid, but in its dilute form it is an excellent pickle.

    Citric acid is slower to clean the metal, but is safer; it is readily
bought from chemists and supermarkets, as the packet shown in
Figure 46. It is available in liquid or in powder form ready for you to
dissolve it in water. A mix of 25g of citric acid monohydrate to 250ml
is sufficient to pickle a burner. Sulphuric acid is most easily found on
the Internet or extracted as acid from an old battery. Do not even
think about buying concentrated acid. A 10 per cent concentration or
thereabouts is quite sufficient for a pickle. Figure 47 shows an old
5ltr (1gal) container of dilute acid.
   Please make sure you wear eye protection and gloves when
handling sulphuric acid. If for any reason you get acid on your skin,
quickly wash with cold water to prevent your skin being affected by
the acid. If you get any in your eye, immediately rinse thoroughly
with saline solution rather than tap water.

FIG. 48
      Pickling a soldered 28mm burner in a plastic box filled with dilute sulphuric acid.

    Typically, a burner will clean up nicely in sulphuric acid in half to
one hour as shown in Figure 48, while immersion in citric acid
requires several hours. Once removed from the pickle, rinse the item
several times in fresh water, dry, and then clean off any residual
coating with wire wool before polishing any brass parts that will not
be painted.



  DISPOSING OF UNWANTED SULPHURIC ACID

   Before discarding any old or unwanted acid, just add sodium
   bicarbonate – ordinary baking powder – to neutralize it and
   render it inert. Thus you will eliminate the possibility of burning
   yourself or anyone else, and it can safely go down the drain.

   Burners for model steam boilers with centre flues running along
their length need to operate when mounted horizontally, and must fit
snugly over the end of the flue. Thus the popular sizes of flue

diameter – 42mm, 35mm and 28mm – will need different-sized
burners, shown in Figure 49, to produce the optimum heat output.
However, for boilers with imperial or other ‘non-standard’ size flues, it
is easy to fabricate a suitable adaptor ring, shown fitted to the left-
hand burner in Figure 49.





                                      FIG. 50
 A 35mm burner fitted to an Ahoy 108mm (41⁄4in) horizontal boiler that has eight Galloway
                                  tubes in the flue.

Three of the burners described in this chapter are an easy push
fit on to the end of the boiler flue. Figure 50 shows a 108mm
diameter horizontal boiler with a 35mm burner fitted over its flue.
However, occasionally a flue may need a ‘male’ rather than a
‘female’ burner to fit into, rather than over the flue. The method of
doing this is shown for the 28mm burner. A similar modification to
both the two larger burners can easily be applied. And for different
flue sizes, an adaptor can be made from a short length of brass rod.
   Each of these burners can be readily made from two different
sizes of copper plumbing stop ends, a length of copper tube or brass
rod, a ceramic honeycomb disc and a short length of 1⁄2in or 12mm
brass rod. Some ceramic adhesive filler will also be needed to fix the
ceramic element in place.
   The parts of the burners must be silver soldered as soft solder
will not be strong enough at the temperatures experienced. The
smallest burner should provide sufficient heat for a 75mm (3in)
boiler, the 35mm burner for 90mm (31⁄2in) to 100mm (4in) diameter
ones, and the largest 42mm burner for 108mm (41⁄4in) and any other
similar size boilers.
   The metals used to build the burners, unlike those used to build
model boilers, are not subjected to any pressures or continuous
exposure to steam and hot water. As LPG fuel passes through them,
they do need to have their joints sealed, and of course they will be
exposed to considerable heat. Finally, the length of the inner tube
holding the ceramic element can be altered to suit the flue. It can be
made a little longer or shorter if required, depending on how far the
flue tube sticks out of the boiler.

FIG. 51
          Eight secondary air holes are needed in the end cap for a 28mm burner.

   There is debate about whether secondary air holes around the
larger end cap are a benefit. Figure 51 shows an end cap for a
28mm burner with secondary air holes drilled around its end. Some
manufacturers include these air holes, others do not. Tests with the
three sizes of burner in this chapter showed that excluding
secondary air holes in the larger two burners improved the heat

output to the boiler and also reduced potential whistling in the flue.
Figure 52 shows early 35mm and 28mm burners with secondary air
holes used in the tests. However, contrary to expectation, the 28mm
burner still needs secondary air holes to burn correctly. The larger
two burners clearly get sufficient secondary air through the primary
air holes, while for the smallest burner, the air flow appears to be
insufficient and secondary air holes will need to be included.





                                      FIG. 52
An early prototype 35mm burner with twelve secondary air holes drilled around its perimeter
                 beside a 28mm burner with eight secondary air holes.

   Testing was carried out with burners with secondary air holes
fitted to horizontal boiler flues to check the temperature of the hot air
coming out of the chimney, and the time taken for a cold boiler to
reach its working temperature. This was then repeated with the
secondary air holes blocked, confirming that both the 42mm and the
35mm burners performed better without secondary air holes.

BRASS GAS-JET HOUSINGS

The gas-jet housings are virtually identical for the 42mm, 35mm and
28mm burners. The housing is the first part to make (see Figure 53).
It consists of a length of 1⁄2in or 12mm brass rod faced each end to
the required length, which varies depending on the size of the
burner; turn down about half its length to 8mm (5⁄16in) to fit the
burner body. Drill it 6mm right through from the narrow end, and then
drill the wide end 8mm (5⁄16in) to a depth of 20mm (25⁄32in). Finally
cross-drill right through 6mm (1⁄4in) for primary air at a point 12.5mm
(1⁄2in) from the wider end, and also drill and tap at a point 6mm (1⁄4in)
from the wide end for a 6BA or M3 bolt to adjust and hold the gas jet
in place. Figure 54 provides the dimensions of the parts.

42mm stop end with a 35mm hole bored in its centre to fit the burner
tube. This tube fits into the smaller 35mm stop end, and they both
have an 8mm (5⁄16 in) hole cross-drilled for the gas-jet housing to

    Fit the larger 42mm end cap in the lathe and drill a hole large
enough to enable the boring bar to be employed, using standard
green Swarfega as a lubricant. Now bore out this centre hole in the
lathe so the length of 35mm copper pipe will pass through it with
about 0.13mm (0.005in) clearance for silver solder. Figure 57 shows
the end cap being bored, while Figure 58 shows a complete set of
machined parts.

FIG. 59

   Carefully clean, flux and assemble the parts ready for silver
soldering. This excludes the bolt that will hold the gas jet in position.
As Figure 59 demonstrates, support the larger end cap, since the

copper tube sticks some 4mm (5⁄32in) below it, ensuring the larger
end cap is up against the smaller end cap. Check that the gap from
the end of the jet housing across to the copper tube is 3mm (1⁄8in).
Flux all the joints as you assemble the items.
    Finally, the whole assembly is ready to be soldered with a hand-
held MAPP gas torch or a propane torch fitted with a small burner.
Run silver solder around the gas-jet housing joint to the smaller end
cap, and the joint of the outer casing to the copper tube and smaller
end cap. When cool, the complete assembly can be pickled,
washed, then any remaining flux cleaned off, and finally any excess
solder removed with a file. Do check that good, gas-tight joints have
been made.

FIG. 60

   To make the ceramic element for the burner, place the 35mm
copper tube on the reverse, flat side of the piece of ceramic material,
and run a pencil round it to make the size of the circle required. Cut

round the material with the ceramic saw, and then file the resulting
circle to size so that it fits into the end cap for just half the thickness
of the ceramic – in effect the round edge should be slightly conical.
The piece of ceramic and the completed burner body can be seen in
Figure 60.
   To glue the ceramic element in the burner, run a thin line of
ceramic adhesive filler around both the inside top of the copper tube
and the lower outer edge of the ceramic disc, push the disc in place,
and clean off any excess adhesive with a damp cloth. If there are
any unfilled gaps between the ceramic and the tube, add more heat-
resistant filler and smooth in place. A little water helps both to
smooth the adhesive and remove it from places where it is not
wanted.

paint; black is ideal. However, the brass can be left bare or polished,
as there are no suitably heat-resistant etch primers. Without such a
primer, any paint on the brass will rapidly start to come off. Figure 61
shows the finished burner.

FIG. 62
   A 42mm burner alight and already, as it warms up, providing a fair amount of heat.

    Finally, fit a No. 8 jet (possibly even a No. 10 jet) in the holder,
and the holder in the gas-jet housing so its end is just over half way
along the primary air hole. Connect the jet to a tank of a

propane/butane mix, check there are no leaks, turn on the gas and
light the flame on the ceramic element. Adjust the position of the jet
and the rate of gas flow so that blue cones form all over the surface,
as demonstrated in Figure 62. Then, wearing heat-resistant gloves,
the burner can be carefully inserted in the flue of the boiler to raise
steam.

the opposite side of the burner. The measurements for the various
components are given in Figure 65.





                                      FIG. 66
                 The five metal components of the 35mm burner.

   Use the lathe to drill a hole in the centre of the 35mm end cap
that forms the outer casing. Then the centre hole can be bored out
so the length of 28mm copper pipe will pass through it with about
0.13mm (0.005in) clearance. Figure 66 shows all the metal parts
ready for assembly.

FIG. 67
    Silver soldering the four metal components of a 35mm burner (excluding the bolt that
                         secures the gas-jet holder in place).

  Make sure that all the parts have been cleaned, fluxed and
assembled so they are ready to be silver soldered. The larger end
cap will have to be supported since the copper tube sticks 9mm
(3⁄8in) below it. Ensure the larger cap is a snug fit with the smaller

end cap. Check that the gap between the end of the jet housing and
the inside of the copper tube is 3mm (1⁄8in). Now silver solder the
whole assembly with the gas torch, ensuring that silver solder runs
round the gas-jet housing join to the small end cap and the join of
the large end cap, the copper tube and the small end cap. Figure 67
shows the original burner being soldered.
   Once the assembly is cool, the complete burner can be pickled,
carefully washed and dried; then clean off any flux, file or emery off
any excess solder, and check for good, gas-tight joints.

FIG. 68
  The ceramic element is ready to be glued into the cleaned-up body of a 35mm burner.

   To make the size of the ceramic needed, mark its back with a
pencil using the 28mm tube as a template, then saw it roughly to
size. File the resulting circle of ceramic to a slight taper so it fits into
the end cap. About half the thickness of the ceramic should be in the

copper tube and half sticking out. Figure 68 shows the ceramic disc
and the soldered burner body.
   To glue the ceramic into the burner body, place a small amount of
ceramic adhesive filler round the inside top of the copper tube and
round the ceramic disc, and then press the disc firmly in place.
Remove excess adhesive and fill any gaps between the element and
the copper tube with a bit more filler. Then smooth in place. Some
water and a damp cloth will help to smooth the glue so any excess
can be cleaned off.
   The look of the burner can be improved by painting its outer
copper parts with black heatresistant paint. However, leave the brass
part bare and polish it, as no heat-resistant etch primers are
available. Without a primer, any paint on the brass is unlikely to last
long in good condition.

FIG. 69
 The heat of the flame is now starting to show above the blue cones on the 35mm burner.

    Fit a No. 8 jet in the holder, and place the holder in the gas-jet
housing so the jet fills just over half the primary air hole. Connect the
jet to the gas tank, check to ensure there are no leaks, turn on the
gas and light the ceramic element. Adjust the jet’s position and the
rate of gas flow so blue cones, as those shown in Figure 69, form on
the surface: now you are in business!

28MM (1 7⁄64 IN) BURNER

This smallest burner is made in a similar way to the two larger ones,
but uses 28mm and 22mm end caps. However, a length of 22mm
copper tube is not acceptable as it leaves insufficient space between
the flue and the tube. As a result, turn a 43mm (111⁄16 in) length of
25mm or 1in brass down to a diameter of 22mm (155⁄64 in). Then turn
one end down to 20.5mm (113⁄16in) for a length of 25mm (1in).
Finally, bore to a diameter of 19mm (3⁄4in). While turning, check that
the broad end fits into the small end cap. The ceramic element will
glue into the slimmer end (see Figure 70). The measurements of the
various parts can be obtained from Figure 71.





                                      FIG. 70
        The completed 28mm burner, clearly showing the secondary air holes.

FIG. 71
The sizes of the components, apart from the gas-jet housing, that are required to make a
                     28mm ceramic burner.

FIG. 72
            Using a 6mm slot drill to form the eight holes in a 28mm end cap.

    Drill a hole in the centre of the 28mm end cap using Swarfega as
a lubricant, so it can be bolted to the rotary table with a suitably sized
spacer. Ensure the centre of the rotary table is under the
millingmachine-chuck centre line. Tilt the table to 45 degrees, and
move the whole table along the X-axis until a 6mm (1⁄4in) mill or

copper drill in the chuck is directly over the location of the first hole.
The set-up can be seen in Figure 72. Lock the milling machine and
rotary table and drill the first hole. Turn the rotary table through 45
degrees, relock it and drill the second hole. Repeat every 45 degrees
to form eight holes in the larger end cap, each 6mm (1⁄4in) diameter
and 45 degrees apart.





                                      FIG. 73
  The five metal component parts of the 28mm burner, together with the disc of ceramic.

   Next, bore out the central hole to 22mm (7⁄8in) in the lathe, again
providing some 0.13mm (0.005in) clearance for silver solder. Locate

the larger end of the turned brass tube in the small end cap, and mill
or drill an 8mm (5⁄16in) hole in the copper end cap and the brass tube
12.5mm (1⁄2in) from its bottom for the gas-jet housing. The gas-jet
housing is the same as the one for the other burners, but the
narrower end is shorter at 19mm (3⁄4in) to maintain a gap to the edge
of the housing at about 3mm (1⁄8in). Figure 73 shows a complete set
of machined parts.

FIG. 74
             The main parts of the 28mm burner being silver soldered.

  Now all the parts can be carefully cleaned, fluxed and fitted
together. Silver soldering is straightforward as the change in

diameter of the inner tube ensures that the parts locate in the correct
position. When inverted, the large end cap may need some 3mm
(1⁄8in) supports to keep it steady. Now heat the whole assembly until
the flux flows and the metal starts to glow red. Run silver solder
around the gas-jet housing joint to the smaller end cap, as illustrated
in Figure 74, and the joint of the outer casing to the brass tube and
smaller end cap. When it has cooled, the complete assembly should
be pickled, washed, and then any excess flux cleaned off; remove
any surplus solder, and check that gas-tight joints have been made.
   To make the ceramic element, place the 22mm brass tube on the
reverse, flat side of the piece of ceramic, and mark a circle the size
needed. Cut the material with the ceramic saw, and then file the
edge of the resulting disc to the slightly conical shape that fits into
the end cap for just half its thickness.

FIG. 75
          The cleaned-up 28mm burner with its ceramic element ready to fit.

   At this stage, shown in Figure 75, the ceramic element can be
glued into the burner. Run a thin strip of adhesive filler around both
the inner top of the brass tube and the ceramic, press the ceramic
disc in place, and clean off excess filler with a damp cloth. Check for

unfilled gaps between the element and the brass tube. If there are
any, add some more filler, smooth it down and clean off any
remaining excess.

FIG. 76
        A completed 28mm burner needing only a gas-jet holder and gas jet.

   Improve the look of the burner by painting its outer copper parts
with black or coloured heat-resistant paint. Leave the brass parts

bare or polished, because without a high-temperature etch primer,
any paint on the brass will quickly start to look shabby. The finished
burner can be seen in Figure 76.

FIG. 77
    The 28mm burner alight and correctly set up, showing blue cones and a hot flame.

   At last a No. 5 jet can be fitted in the holder and the holder in the
gas-jet housing so the jet is half way along the primary air hole.

Connect a gas tank of a propane/butane mix, check there are no
leaks, turn on the gas and light the top of the ceramic element.
Adjust the position of the jet and gas flow so that blue cones form on
the surface. Heat will rapidly be generated, as can be seen in Figure
77, and you are finally ready to go.

Trevithick 1⁄16 scale dredger engine and boiler. The flue has an
internal diameter of 28mm, but unfortunately does not stick out
beyond the boiler end plate. This is shown in Figure 78. The need,
therefore, was for a burner that would plug into, rather than over the

       HIS CHAPTER COVERS THE building of two different sizes of round
      burner and two different shapes of rectangular burner, with
     one variant. All four are designed to fit in the firebox of either aT
vertical or horizontal boiler of the appropriate size. Full dimensions
are given of all the components, and how they can be assembled to
provide working burners for vertical and horizontal boilers that have
a firebox.

FIG. 82
Two round and three rectangular burners. Their sizes and shapes suit a wide range of boiler
                                          fireboxes.

FIG. 83

   Ceramic burners for vertical and horizontal model steam boilers
built without a centre flue can be either round or rectangular,
depending on the size and shape of the boiler firebox, which must
include an adequate number of secondary air holes. Figure 82

shows all five of these burners, while Figure 83 shows a boiler that
needs a circular burner and Figure 84 is an example of one that uses
a rectangular burner to provide heat. All except one of the burners
are significantly larger than the 42mm, 35mm and 28mm ones
described in the previous chapter.
   The round burners are again based on plumbing end caps. The
rectangular ones can be folded from 1.6mm (16 SWG) copper or
brass sheet, with dimensions to suit the size of the boiler firebox.
The round burners are ideal for vertical boilers up to 108mm (41⁄4in)
diameter, and the rectangular ones for similar-sized horizontal
boilers.

         The simple set of parts needed to mount a burner in a boiler firebox.

   Both types of burner require a brass gas-jet housing with holes
for primary air, and the ability to adjust the position of the gas-jet
holder in the housing. In addition, a length of stainless-steel spring

and a small piece of stainless-steel mesh are needed as gas-
diffusion components. Mounting the burner in a boiler requires a
simple mount of the type shown in Figure 85. It is easily machined
from brass strip; dimensions are given in Figure 188 on page 90.

GAS-JET HOUSINGS

The gas-jet housings for the 54mm and 67mm round burners and
the three rectangular burners are identical. Figure 86 gives the
dimensions, while Figure 87 shows a completed housing. They are
made from 12.5mm (1⁄2in) brass rod, drilled 8mm and faced each
end to 46mm (113⁄16in) long.

diameter to fit in the hole in the burner body. Cross-drill a 6mm (1⁄4in)
hole right through the housing, 19mm (3⁄4in) from the other end, and
a second 6mm (1⁄4in) hole drilled only in the top of the housing, also
19mm (3⁄4in) from the same end. Drill and tap a 6BA or M3 hole,
6mm (1⁄4in) from the end for the short bolt that holds the jet in
position. The housing can then be silver soldered into its round or
rectangular housing, but first remove the bolt.

Figure 88 shows the complete 67mm and 54mm round burners.

and a hole drilled for the gas-jet housing. This drilling is easily done
by clamping the body to an angle plate (see Figure 94), or holding it

position with fire bricks so the gas-jet housing stands upright for
soldering. With flux around the joint, it only requires a fairly quick
touch of silver-solder rod to complete the joint. Once it is completely
cool, any flux can be removed, and the whole assembly cleaned in

60mm (23⁄8in) long for the smaller one. In addition, a strip of twenty-
mesh (twenty holes per inch with a 1.02mm aperture and 0.25mm
wire diameter as a woven wire mesh) stainless-steel mesh
measuring 15mm (9⁄16in) × 40mm (11⁄2in) is needed. Figures 95 and

pencil, using the burner body as a template. Then cut out the circle
and carefully file or sand it so it just fits in the burner body with 6mm
(1⁄4in) sticking above the rim. Glue it in place by spreading ceramic
adhesive filler around the inside rim of the burner body and the lower

Figure 104 shows two larger rectangular burners, which are a
nominal 70 × 50mm (23⁄4 × 2in), and a smaller one that measures 65

Cut out the shape of the burner housing from copper sheet with the
four corners removed, as shown in Figure 105. A choice has to be
made about whether to fold the boxes with the metal as supplied, or
after it has been annealed. It requires rather more force to bend

unannealed metal, but the base and sides tend to be flatter.
Annealed metal is much easier to bend but tends to distort, though
judicious use of a soft-headed hammer readily removes any
blemishes. Figure 106 provides the dimensions of the larger
rectangular burner. Note that the long sides extend 3mm (1⁄8in)
beyond the base to allow overlapping corners. Cut the short length
between the long sides and the base so that the ends can be
correctly folded.

INSTALLING A SMALL CERAMIC BURNER IN A
VEHICLE SUCH AS A STEAM ROLLER

Installing a small ceramic burner in a static engine is quite
straightforward, but installing one in a vehicle such as a steam
roller can be a little more problematic. Assuming you have
selected the shape of burner to fit in the firebox, you will need
the smallest refillable gas tank you can find. A small vertical
tank is easily installed on the back of the vehicle by bolting a
pair of small Terry clips to its back end.
   With the tank fitted and the burner in place, use a short
length of soft wire to run along the route the gas pipe will
follow. Measure the length, and then cut the same length of
1⁄8in copper pipe, and bend the pipe to the desired shape.
Silver solder a gas-jet holder to one end, and a connector to
the gas tank on the other. Then fit the gas-jet holder in the
housing, and connect the other end to the gas tank to check
the layout.
  Remove the burner and gas tank, and connect them
together with the gas jet in roughly the right place so that you
can turn on the gas, light the burner and adjust the position of
the jet and the gas valve to get the desired flame. Tighten the
bolt that locates the gas-jet holder in place in its housing.
  Now turn off the gas, allow the burner to cool, and refit the
burner in the firebox and the gas tank in its clips. Connect the
pipe to the gas tank, and check to see if you need to make a
small clip to hold the burner securely in position.

Good steaming!

Liquefied Petroleum Gas
                          6
                     (LPG)


       HIS CHAPTER LOOKS AT the various aspects of using liquefied
      petroleum gas (LPG) to heat ceramic burners. It covers the
      features of the various gases, how best to contain them, andT
which are best suited to heating small steam boilers. Various safety
issues are discussed, and it is important to apply them. Finally, the
chapter also provides information about small gas containers and
refillable tanks.
   As mentioned at the start of Chapter 2, LPG is used in many
applications, including silver soldering. It is also a popular heat
source for small steam boilers. For heating these boilers, the gas is
available as propane, butane, or as a mixture of the two. It has an
unpleasant smell so leaks can be easily detected. LPG burns readily
and is denser than air so it pools in low areas. Any leaks present a
fire risk. While the physical properties of butane and propane are
similar, both gases are poisonous, although butane is less toxic than
propane and can be legally stored indoors.
   The difference in the properties of propane and butane means
that they are particularly suited to specific uses. Propane’s lower
boiling point of –42ºC suits outdoor use. Butane does not work well
in colder conditions, only vaporizing just above –2ºC, and is best
used indoors or outside in the summer months. Otherwise the
performance of the two gases is very similar in terms of flame
temperature and calorific value.

LPG can be compressed into very small cylinders. It changes
easily to a liquid under pressure, so reasonable amounts of gas can
be stored in a relatively small volume. However, to work in a ceramic
burner, the LPG must be able to boil into a gas. Liquid propane
expands 250 times when it turns from a liquid to a gas. When LPG is
released from its pressurized canister, it boils, turns into a gas, and
in doing so cools the liquid in the container. Thus the LPG
temperature will drop some way below ambient, and this can prevent
butane alone from boiling and so producing a useful gas supply,
even when the outside temperature is significantly above freezing.
This can still be a problem with a propane/butane mix when, for
example, sailing a steam-powered boat on a cold, windy day.
   The ceramic burners described in this book are all designed to
run on LPG. Of the various types of LPG, a butane and propane
mixture, typically 70/30, sometimes with isobutane, is the preferred
fuel to be used in ceramic burners suitable for heating model steam
boilers. To provide the gas for the burner either a small disposable
canister can be used, or a refillable gas tank can be fitted, and
loaded with gas from one of the larger disposable cans. Always fill
any refillable tank out of doors so that any inevitable leakage
dissipates safely.
    In northern Europe, especially in the winter months, the best
compromise is the mix of propane and butane commonly found in
the small gas cartridges produced for camping stoves and gas
lamps. This mix is widely available in small- and medium-size
disposable canisters. These canisters can be bought from DIY,
camping and caravan equipment stores.
   Experience has shown that in operation, particularly in cold
weather, gas cylinders can quickly become so cold that their output
pressure and rate of gas flow can fall to the point where insufficient
heat is available from the burner to keep the boiler steaming at the
rate required to drive its engine. For static installations, the solution

is simple: place the gas cylinder in a bowl of warm water, and the
gas flow will almost immediately increase to its normal level. For
installations in boats and land vehicles, the solution is rather harder.
One answer is to feed warm air around the gas tank. An option is to
install a small electric fan to blow warm air into the compartment
containing the gas tank. Another alternative that can help is to run a
copper strip from beneath the boiler’s burner to the gas tank to
conduct heat from one to the other.
   For those who prefer a gas tank integrated into the system,
particularly for model boat use, a number of designs are available
from model engineering suppliers. For those who want a system that
controls the gas flow to the burner as the pressure in the boiler
varies, one of several commercially available solutions can be
purchased, both electronic and mechanical. These are described in
Chapter 8.



  BASIC SAFETY NOTICE

   Here is yet another ‘health and safety’ warning that you
   should read. Remember to be careful when working with your
   ceramic burner. Some essential safety precautions need to be
   observed when using LPG as a fuel for a burner, since it is a
    potential danger if it is misused.

  ■ Connectors and their associated pipes must be installed
      correctly, and it is essential to check there are no leaks.
     Apply soapy water to all joints, and when you turn the gas
     on, check that no bubbles form. All joints should be
     inspected frequently to avoid future problems
  ■ LPG is denser than air and will pool in any enclosed area.
     This includes your workshop, your car or other vehicle, and

the inside of your model. Therefore tanks should always be
       refilled in the open air
  ■ Always use a butane/propane mix. Once a gas tank has
    been filled, or if the burner fails to ignite and the gas is
     turned off, allow time for any spilled gas to disperse before
     any attempt is made to light or re-light the burner
  ■ Ensure that you always shut off the gas valve after use, and
    remove the connection to any disposable can

  CONTAINER SAFETY TESTING

   At least every five years, safety checks must be carried out on
   any refillable gas tank to check for leaks. Disposable tanks
   are exempt from this requirement. Remove the tank from its
   location in your model, and also remove any covering, but
   leave the gas filler valve and gas control valve in place. The
    test involves filling the tank with your usual LPG, and raising
   the gas mixture to approximately 20ºC to test for leaks from
   the fittings. This is most easily done by immersing the tank in
   a bucket of water at 20ºC and checking for bubbles.
    A soap-bubble test is more sensitive, and involves
   spraying or painting the complete tank with a mix of water,
    liquid soap and glycerine. Bubbles formed by gas escaping
   indicate a leak. This test can be carried out with cladding on
   the tank. Any observable leak is regarded as a failure, and the
   tank and fittings must be repaired and then re-submitted for a
    further safeguard test. However, a slow leak from the gas

valve to the gas jet is not a reason for failure, but requires a
valve change.

7 Operating the Burners


       ETTING UP A BURNER is critical to the success of steaming any
       boiler and powering an engine. Advice is given on the size of
      gas jet to use with each burner, how to make a gas-jet holder,S
and how to adjust the position of the jet and the gas flow to it in order
to give the optimum heat output from the burner and avoid causing
damage to it. Details are also included of installing burners and their
pipework, as well as lighting the burner.
   Before a new burner is mounted in a boiler, screw the
recommended size of jet into the jet holder with a small amount of
sealant. Then slide the holder into the brass housing, connect the
gas to the holder, and check for gas leaks. There is quite a lot to do if
the burner is to work correctly and produce the required amount of
heat. In all cases, the way a burner is set up is critical to its efficient
operation. It must be fitted with the correct size of gas jet, and it is
essential to ensure that the right volume of gas is passing to the
burner, and to adjust the mix of the gas with the primary air to the
ideal setting by moving the gas-jet holder to the optimum position in
the gas-jet housing, so that the burner flame is the right size and
colour.

Gas jets for the ceramic burner you have built come in a range of
sizes: 3, 5, 8, 10, 12 and 16. The larger the number, the larger the

hole in the jet, and the more gas that can flow through it. Even so,
the holes are very small.

LIGHTING THE BURNER

While in theory it should be easy to light a gas burner, in practice it is
not quite as straightforward. For vertical boilers, the burner is hidden
in the firebox and can be lit in one of two ways. With the chimney or
funnel removed, as shown in Figure 171, a flame can be applied to
the top of the boiler as the gas is turned on. Alternatively a flame can
be passed through one of the secondary air holes into the firebox if
access to this part of the boiler is possible. In both cases a clear
‘pop’ will indicate that the burner has lit, and carefully looking down
the chimney or through the secondary air holes will confirm that the
burner is alight.

   The situation for a burner that plugs into the flue of a horizontal
boiler is very different, as lighting from the top of the chimney often
fails to ignite the burner. Tests were made with a glow plug, as used
in model internal combustion engines. The plug glowed a bright
red/yellow when connected to a low voltage battery and was
installed at the other end of the flue to the burner. Unfortunately the
experiment proved to be a total failure and the gas never ignited.
While spark ignition might have worked, the complexity and expense
of such a solution made it impractical.

addition, lighting the burner outside the flue means that heat-
resistant gloves must be used when lighting the burner and pushing
it back into the flue. (See Figure 172.)

three hands protected with heat-resistant gloves. You have to hold
the gas-jet housing making sure not to cover the air holes, while at
the same time positioning the gas jet correctly and tightening the
bolt.) Finally retighten the screw to secure the jet holder firmly in

place. This will ensure the optimum air/gas mixture is obtained. The
resulting correct flame can be seen in Figure 181.

bright red, as Figure 182 demonstrates, and after a while the burner

which can quickly damage the burner. This only seems to occur
when using some commercially built ceramic burners, but it probably
also applies to other types of ceramic burner.

   The way to avoid this is to move the gas jet in a little until a
blue/purple flame is observed, and not an overall red glow. This way,
good heat is produced and the burner will work properly without
overheating. Do not move the jet holder any further out as this will
result in a blue flame moving on the burner surface, which indicates
rather too much air. Figure 183 shows the view through the
secondary air holes of a vertical boiler where the burner flame is set
correctly, while Figure 184 shows the burner glowing bright red,
when it is in danger of destroying itself.
   Note that if a jet is partially blocked, or if there is any other similar
problem with the gas tap or gas pipe, or gas leaking around the jet
threads, problems may also occur, and it may be impossible to
adjust the burner to give a correct flame.
   Once the burner has been warmed, the ceramic will start to burn
with brilliant blue cones, the flame will become purple, and the heat
output will rise. At this point heat transfer to the water in the boiler
will be optimal, and you can wait until the pressure gauge starts to
rise, indicating that steam is being generated.

Clearly it is much easier to set up the burner before plugging it
into the flue or placing it in the firebox. Once the ideal gas-jet
position has been established, fully tighten the securing screw and
try the burner in the boiler.

Burner Blowback

On any of the burners that fit under boilers, rather than fit into
horizontal flues, burner blowback is indicated by a sudden roaring
noise. This means that the flame is now also burning beneath the
ceramic, and it will rapidly damage and then destroy parts of the
burner. Immediately turn off the gas and allow the burner to cool
down. (Interestingly, this phenomenon has not been found to occur
with burners that plug into flues.)

FIG. 185
A commercial 2in (51mm) round burner, with its gas-diffusion components totally destroyed
                                 by blowback.

FIG. 186
 The same commercial 2in (51mm) round burner with its ceramic honeycomb and gas-
diffusion components replaced. It looks good after repair in the author’s home workshop.

FIG. 187
  The commercial 2in (51mm) round burner is burning well, although the gas tap could be
                                    closed a little.

  Damage can involve crumbling of the ceramic element, or even
breaks in any gas diffusing components, such as a spring and wire
mesh. Fortunately it is not a difficult task to replace any of these
parts and fix new ones in place, though it will normally require fitting
at least a new ceramic element. Figure 185 shows a commercial
burner relit after it suffered from blowback and its internal parts were
seriously damaged, while Figure 186 shows the same burner
repaired using a custom-cut piece of ceramic honeycomb. In Figure
187 the whole ceramic element is producing heat after what was a
relatively simple repair.
   Experiments suggest that the cause of burner blowback is
normally too much primary air. To avoid blowback, always set the
gas-jet holder further in than the optimum, and then carefully and
slowly move it further out to get the best possible blue flame. If you
have experienced blowback, before attempting to relight the burner,
make sure that the gas-jet holder is moved a little further into its
housing. After relighting the burner, recheck the flame and readjust
the position of the gas jet in the housing until it is burning correctly.

Boiler Howling

Any horizontal boiler with a flue, into which the burner is plugged,
has the potential to howl. The problem is caused by the acoustic
characteristics of the flue and chimney/funnel combination. Its
length, any obstructions such as Galloway tubes, super heater or
bends, can interact with the velocity of gas and air flow through the
flue. It may also be altered by changes in atmospheric conditions
such as humidity, pressure and temperature. While howling is not an

uncommon problem, it is relatively straightforward to solve by trial
and error.
   You can try increasing the size of the gas jet and reducing the
flow at the gas valve. These two measures should enable you to set
the blue cones on the burner, but with the speed of the gas coming
out of the jet reduced. Increasing the gas jet one or two sizes should
quickly resolve the problem without altering the heat output of the
burner. It is a simple question of balancing the variables, jet size, the
amount the gas valve is open, and the associated air flow and the
amount of noise from the flue. However, do warm up the flue first at
a low gas setting before any work to eliminate howling is carried out.

BURNER INSTALLATION

After setting up the burner correctly, turn off the gas so the burner
can cool before installing it in the firebox of the boiler or plugging it
into the flue. It is essential that plenty of fresh secondary air can
enter the flue or firebox. Only the smallest 28mm burners have
secondary air holes bored in their outer casings – the other flue-
mounted burners obtain sufficient secondary air through the gas-jet
housing.
   The larger burners and the two smallest flatbottomed ones sit in
the fireboxes of their boilers. It is important to ensure that these
fireboxes have ample air holes. Too much air is not a problem, but
too little will inhibit effective burning, will reduce heat output, and in
severe cases, can cause damage to the burner.

PIPEWORK AND VALVES

When connecting a gas source to a boiler burner take care that the
joints are all gas tight. It is sensible to apply soapy water to each
joint and to ensure that when the gas is on, it is not blowing any
bubbles. A manual gas valve that is screwed on to a disposable gas
tank, or a similar valve fitted to a refillable gas tank, controls the gas
flow. Normally 1⁄8in outsidediameter copper pipe should be used to
connect the gas to the burner. One end usually terminates in a
manual screw fitting that goes on to the gas valve; the other joins to
the gas jet holder. However, sometimes you will need to use 1⁄4mm ×
40ME coned connectors.

FIG. 191
 Commercial steam plant in an attractive launch with the burner and gas tank both visible.

   To make a neat pipe run, a pipe bender such as the one shown in
Figure 21 on page 19 should be used. A very tidy marine installation
can be seen in Figure 191, where all the various steam and gas
pipes are neatly fitted in place. The steam pipes have ‘fake’ asbestos
insulation covering them.

For static installations and also for testing burners and boilers, a
flexible gas pipe can be a great advantage. It is ideal for connecting
burners that plug into a round flue, allowing you to light the burner
before plugging it into the flue using protective gloves. It is also an
advantage for some static installations where the burners sit in the
boiler firebox, as the gas cylinder can be readily moved to the
preferred position.
  A manual gas valve will only allow the heat input to be set to
match the expected steam output to the engine approximately. A
radio-controlled gas-tight valve driven by a servo will give rather
better boilerpressure management. Alternatively, a commercial gas
regulator can be fitted, which varies the gas flow to maintain the
steam pressure in the boiler. The next chapter gives more
information about these options.

GAS SEALANTS

When installing gas jets and connecting up gas pipework, the use of
a gas sealant is recommended to make the joints gas tight. Loctite
542, Heldite or Rocol pipe-jointing compound are all suitable and
only need smearing on the joints to provide a gas-tight seal. They
are available from plumbers’ merchants and DIY stores.

IGNITERS

Matches or a lighter can be used to ignite a burner in a vertical
boiler, but a better solution is to use an igniter such as the one
shown in Figure 192. These igniters burn lighter fuel (butane), which
can be easily topped up from a lighter-fuel can. Ignition of the gas is
by a piezo-electric crystal. The burner in a vertical boiler can be lit by
removing the chimney, holding the lit igniter to the chimney mount,

and turning on the gas. A distinctive ‘pop’ will indicate that the burner
has been safely lit.

Gas Control 8


          HILE THE GAS CONTROL to a burner can always be set up
         manually, this chapter describes a number of mechanical
        and electronic automatic gas-control systems that areW
much more important where the steam plant is fitted in a vehicle or
boat. A number of different systems are described so that an
informed choice can be made; also described is a radio-controlled
gas cut-off valve.

FIG. 193
  A 54mm round burner heating a 102mm (4in) vertical boiler for a test run with a small
                                  single-cylinder mill engine.

   Any ceramic burner requires a gas tank to hold its fuel, but some
sort of gas-control system will also be needed. This may be just a
simple on/off valve that is built into, or screws on to the gas tank,
with a pipe that runs to the gas jet in the burner (see Figure 193).
Such a valve can be used, partly open, to set the rate of gas flow

manually. This can only be done by looking at the burner, although
this can be difficult in some installations. For running a static steam
engine and boiler combination in the workshop, this is usually an
adequate approach. However, it is less than satisfactory in a mobile
application such as a steam launch or a small steam lorry. Thus your
chosen solution may also be a more complex one that senses boiler
pressure and varies the gas flow to the burner in order to maintain
the required pressure.
   The type and size of gas tank depends both on individual choice
and on the environment in which the burner is intended to be used.
For a static application, a disposable gas-can with a simple gas
valve can be fitted; the valve can then be manually operated to
increase or decrease the gas flow to the burner and thus maintain
pressure in the boiler as the engine consumes steam. Equally a
refillable gas tank with a similar gas valve can be fitted.
    In both cases, if the safety valve starts to lift with the engine
running, it is a simple matter to turn down the gas flow so that the
ceramic burner provides rather less heat to the boiler. Similarly the
gas flow can be turned up if the boiler pressure starts to fall. All this
assumes that the boiler and engine are a good match.
   For marine applications and for small-scale steam lorries and
traction engines, as well as small-gauge locomotives and other
mobile applications, it is essential that the gas supply is exhausted
before all the water in the boiler has been used. This implies fitting a
relatively small gas tank to supply the burner. Its size depends on the
water capacity of the boiler it heats, whether a boiler feed pump is
fitted to the engine, and the volume of its water supply as well as the
size of the engine, its steam consumption, and the way it is
operated. An oscillating engine will always have a significantly higher
steam consumption than a side-valve one and will require more heat
from the burner, all other things being equal.

Do you plan to run your engine mostly at full power, or much of
the time well throttled back, or even at times stationary? Think about
these variables carefully and decide the size of the gas tank
accordingly.
   Having chosen the gas tank, a connector and valve will be
needed regardless of whether a boiler pressure-control system is
fitted as well. The decision to install one is often price dependent, as
a complex gas-control installation is not cheap.

AUTOMATIC BOILER CONTROL

There are several commercial solutions that aim to provide a
constant boiler steam pressure regardless of steam consumption.
There are both electronic and mechanical systems that fit between
the boiler and the gas tank. An electronic gas valve automatically
controls gas flow to the burner using a pressure sensor fitted to the
boiler. It reduces the gas flow to just a pilot when the pressure is
sufficient. The chosen pressure can be set with a screwdriver
adjustment on the electronic control box. However, a servo will have
to be provided in order to move the gas valve, although this servo
will not be connected to, and will operate independently from, any
radiocontrol system that may be fitted.
   The alternative mechanical solutions use a flexible membrane,
connected to boiler pressure, to control the flow of gas. The required
pressure is set using a simple screw adjustment. The advantages
and disadvantages of the two different types of system and their cost
are likely to affect your choice. When looking at electronic systems,
remember there will be a battery to charge or replace, and the cost
of the extra servo. Balanced against this are the simpler controls that
you may find are easier to adjust on electronic solutions.

ELECTRONIC SYSTEMS

Using a pressure sensor fitted to the boiler and a battery-powered
electronic control box, a servo (independent of any radio-control
system) automatically adjusts gas flow to the burner via a servo-
operated gas valve. The movement of the valve reduces the gas flow
to just a pilot when the pressure is sufficient, and increases it again
when the pressure falls. The chosen pressure can be set with a
screw adjustment on the electronic control box.

Stuart Electronic Gas Valve (EGV)

The Stuart EGV comprises six items, which, when correctly
connected together, aim to regulate the gas flow to the burner. They
are the pressure sensor, the control box, the gas valve, the gas
connecting pipe, the battery holder, the switch and the wiring cable.
A four-page leaflet covers the installation and setting up.

in response to signals from the control box. Four fully charged AA

32 ME threaded bush on the boiler with the usual sealing

terminals 1 and 2 on the control box. The red and black wires from

(you provide the servo) and sets the gas flow to the burner. The
knurled knob is used to set the gas flow to the pilot so that, even with

The gas jet in the burner needs a gas pipe and connector, which can
be screwed into the valve output.

MECHANICAL SYSTEMS

All the mechanical solutions use flexible membranes inside a gas-
pressure regulator valve. One end connects via a steam pipe to a
fitting on the boiler in order to sense the steam pressure and thus
control the flow of gas. The required boiler pressure is set using a
thumb-wheel adjustment on the regulator valve. Figure 199 shows
typical examples of these solutions. When the desired pressure is
reached, the regulator reduces gas flow to a pilot and vice-versa
when the steam pressure falls. There are several different valves
available that all work on a similar principle.

Antón in France produces a similar mechanical solution, as does
Microcosm from China.

However, these last two use a different layout to the Bix solution. All
the devices automatically vary the burner flame to try and maintain
the boiler pressure. However, the Bix burner does not have an
adjustment to set the pilot flame; the other two do. In practice it may
be slightly tricky to ensure the burner operates satisfactorily under
changing gas settings.

the control wheel, the gas supply to the burner is reduced to an

GAS CUT-OFF VALVES

When installing a steam plant in a boat, the question of safety arises:
how do you turn off the gas if the boiler runs out of water? The
solution is to use a radio-controlled cut-off gas valve: this requires an
additional servo, and the risk of battery or radio failure still remains.

Antón Radio-Controlled Gas Shut-Off Valve

The shut-off valve pictured in Figure 206 fits between the gas tank
and the burner or, assuming either a manual or electronic gas
regulator is fitted, either between the regulator and the burner, or
between the gas tank and regulator. The valve is operated by a
radio-control servo. The radio channel should be a switched one so
the valve is either open or closed. It should employ a standard servo
capable of providing a force of 3kg (6.6lb) pushing directly along the
axis of the valve. Antón emphasizes that in the open position, it is
important to ensure the servo arm is in line with the operating rod on
the valve to minimize the power consumption of the servo. Figure
207 shows how to install the valve.

Conclusions


     OU WILL NOW HAVE discovered that, in model engineering terms,
       there is nothing particularly demanding about making a
      ceramic burner. The materials to make the component partsY
are readily available, and the various parts are not difficult to
produce in the home workshop using hand tools and a lathe to make
them. Only for the 28mm burner is access to a milling machine and
rotary table needed.

FIG. 208
       Which of these eleven burners will you choose to build to heat your boiler?

   Figure 208 shows all the burners that you will have read about,
and asks which one you will choose to build. Your choice will really
depend on the size and type of boiler you wish to heat, and whether
it has a flue running through it or a firebox underneath it.
   Assuming you have no basic experience of silver soldering, the
burners described in this book provide an excellent opportunity to

learn this skill as they are not difficult to solder, and do not require a
great amount of heat, nor a large hearth. Hopefully you will feel
sufficiently confident to start building a burner to fit your own boiler,
whether it is a small burner that slots into the flue, or a circular or
rectangular one that is mounted in the firebox.
     It should be apparent that some of the materials for the parts that
are needed to make one burner will actually be sufficient to make a
number of burners. Examples include the honeycomb ceramic, high-
temperature adhesive/filler, and heatproof paint. In addition, end
caps are often supplied in pairs rather than as single items. Thus, if
you can interest friends or fellow club members to build a burner at
the same time as you do, or to use ones that you have built for them,
you can then reduce the overall cost of each individual burner.
   Setting up a burner to optimize its heat output is not difficult, and
only requires the right jet located in the optimum position in the gas-
jet housing, no gas leaks, and the correct amount of flow from the
gas tank. Hopefully the illustrations provided in the book will help you
to achieve the settings correctly so that the heat output of your
burner is optimized.
   Manual control of the burner is fine for a static boiler, but some
form of automatic control of the burner heat output is very desirable,
particularly for use in model boats or land vehicles. 8 has reviewed
the majority of the available systems, both mechanical and
electronic, so it is up to you to decide whether you want one, which
one you would like to fit, and whether you feel that it represents good
value for money.

A tank may be of any shape, with a maximum capacity of 250ml, and
designed to be refillable from a commercial canister of LPG. It shall
be constructed of brass or copper to satisfy the requirements of the
test procedures set out in this code.

The testing shall comprise a hydraulic test followed by a
safeguard test. The object of the hydraulic test is to verify that the
structure of the tank suffers no undue permanent distortion. The
objective of the safeguard test is to verify that the tank is leak proof
at the specified pressure, and that there are no observable leaks
from any fittings. Any observable leak or undue residual distortion of
the tank shall be regarded as a failure.
   Repeat tests shall take place following any repair to the tank, in
which case the tank will be considered new, and the full sequence of
tests described in paragraph 6.1 of the code should be carried out.
   The maker or owner/user must ensure that the tank is only used
with butane or a butane/propane mix below 40 per cent propane,
and never exceeds a temperature of 60ºC. Every tank shall be
indelibly marked with a unique identification number. The form and
position of the marking shall not damage or compromise the
structure of the tank. The tank shall also carry a mark indicating the
type of LPG for which it was constructed.

THE ROLE OF INSPECTORS

Inspectors are appointed by the associations, and may test a tank
only if its maker or current owner/ user is a member of the
associations. Inspectors undertake their duties on a voluntary non-
commercial basis, and all examinations and tests are carried out
entirely at their discretion. Inspectors will only test and certify a tank
that they feel competent to test, based on their own experience. A
test certificate will be issued only by an inspector. Inspectors shall
not inspect their own work, unless that work has already been tested
and passed by another inspector.

HYDRAULIC TEST

The tank should be without fittings, and unmounted in order that it
may be inspected all round. If this is impractical, the agreement of
the inspector will be required before the test can proceed. This
requirement applies to both initial and any subsequent hydraulic
tests.
   The specified initial test pressure for the hydraulic test of the
tank, as described in this code, shall be 400psi gauge pressure. This
will apply for all tanks, regardless of whether they are intended to be
used for butane only, or a butane/propane mix with a maximum
propane content of 40 per cent. The test gauge range should be
approximately 1.5 times the pressure of the test (for example, a
range 0–600psi will be satisfactory for test pressures up to 400psi),
and within the previous two years should have been checked and
calibrated to within ±2 per cent, either against a currently validated
dead-weight test apparatus or against other traceable equipment.
The test gauge may also be calibrated by a commercial test facility,
which will provide a calibration test certificate.

The tank shall be indelibly marked with a unique identification
number. The form and position of the marking shall not damage or
compromise the structure of the tank. The tank shall also carry a
mark indicating the type of LPG for which it was constructed.
   The procedure shall consist of raising the hydraulic pressure from
zero to the test pressure, stopping at several intermediate pressures
for careful visual examination until the full test pressure is attained.
Each test pressure shall be held long enough to investigate any
distortion of the vessel, and to confirm that any fall in pressure is not
caused by structural weakness, and that there are no observable
leaks.

SAFEGUARD TEST

The tank should be unmounted but with the gas filler valve and gas
control valve in place. The tank shall be filled with LPG of a type
specified by the maker or owner/user, and the gas mixture should be
at, or raised to approximately 20ºC to test for leaks from the fittings.
Any observable leak shall be regarded as a failure, and the tank and
fittings shall be repaired and then resubmitted for a further safeguard
test.
    After completion of the hydraulic and safeguard tests, safety
checks shall be carried out on the gas tank at no longer than five-
year intervals, or when the model is next used if greater than that
time interval since previous use.

SAFETY CHECK

A safety check shall be conducted at five-yearly intervals. It shall
take the form of a leak test.

Where reasonably practicable the whole of the tank shall be
examined visually by removal of any covering. Where this is not
possible, the accessible tank joints and unions should be sprayed or
covered with soap solution to reveal any leakage.
   Any leakage observed must be corrected before any further use
of the tank.

CERTIFICATES

The certificate used as part of this code will be given to the
owner/user of the tank for safekeeping, and will be common across,
and available from the associations. Each certificate shall bear the
following information:

■ The name of the club/society and organization issuing the
   certificate
■ The name of the owner/user
■ The location where the test was carried out
■ Identification of the system that the certificate relates to, for
  example the boiler number
■ The maker of the tank
■ The tank identification markings
■ Material(s) used in construction
■ Date of construction, if known
■ Test pressure of the test just completed
■ Signatures of the inspector and the witness
■ Notes and comments where applicable
